title: Pass-by-value and pointer-based updates (C's pass-by-value model)
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C language rules.
Trace the example and explain data flow.
Identify common errors and boundary conditions.
Apply the concept in a small tested program.

understand.concept: C passes arguments by value: the function receives its own parameter object initialized from the argument value. When the value is a pointer, the copied pointer can be used to modify the object it designates, but assigning a new value to the local pointer does not change the caller's pointer.
understand.whyItMatters: This distinction prevents confusion about whether a function can modify a caller's variable or redirect a caller-owned pointer.
understand.analogy: Treat a function or pointer operation as an explicit contract between caller and callee.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for types, object lifetime, scope and linkage.

explain.narrative:
C passes arguments by value: the function receives its own parameter object initialized from the argument value. When the value is a pointer, the copied pointer can be used to modify the object it designates, but assigning a new value to the local pointer does not change the caller's pointer.

When applying this concept, check declared types, preconditions, object lifetime and all control-flow paths. Compile with warnings enabled and test both typical and boundary inputs.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The first call changes only its local parameter copy, so n remains ten. The second call receives an address and changes the object n designates, so n becomes 99.

practise.guidedTask: Predict n after each call and explain which object each function writes.
practise.independentTask: Create a function that changes a caller's integer and another that only changes its local copy.
hints: A pointer argument is still passed by value; the pointed-to object is separately accessible.
To let a function change a caller's pointer, pass a pointer to that pointer.
Use names such as input, output or inout to clarify parameter intent.
